metadata.title: Cuban Missile Crisis Nuclear War Primary-Source Repository
metadata.subtitle: Primary documents for reconstructing what a U.S.-Soviet nuclear war might have looked like in October 1962
metadata.scopeNote: This register compiles publicly available primary documents and authoritative archival listings that bear directly on what would have happened if the Cuban Missile Crisis escalated into U.S.-Soviet nuclear war. Inclusion is limited to documents that show nuclear war plans, casualty or target assumptions, U.S. airstrike or invasion paths, Soviet and Cuban nuclear-use authority, flashpoints that could have triggered nuclear use, or immediate post-crisis evidence about nuclear weapons remaining in Cuba.
metadata.coverageNote: The register is a public-document repository, not a claim that every still-classified or undigitized archival record has been located. Records marked as archival-listing are primary documents identified in official FRUS microfiche source tables but not linked to a public scan here.

documents.title: L.L. Lemnitzer to the President, SIOP 63 Briefing
documents.originator: Lyman L. Lemnitzer / Joint Chiefs of Staff
documents.evidenceRole: Current U.S. general nuclear war plan at the time of the crisis
documents.warQuestion: What strategic nuclear options would President Kennedy have had before him in October 1962?
documents.summary: Briefed Kennedy on SIOP-63 only weeks before the crisis. The document is central because SIOP-63 went into effect on August 1, 1962 and was the U.S. strategic nuclear war plan in force during the missile crisis.
documents.repository: National Archives, RG 218, Records of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, Chairman's Files, Lyman L. Lemnitzer, Box 2
documents.citation: L.L. Lemnitzer to President Kennedy, SIOP 63 Briefing, September 22, 1962.
documents.sourceNote: Posted by the National Security Archive as background document 3 in its SIOP-62/SIOP-63 Nuclear Vault release.

documents.title: History of the Joint Strategic Target Planning Staff: Preparation of SIOP-63
documents.originator: Headquarters, Strategic Air Command, History and Research Division
documents.evidenceRole: Explains the SIOP-63 options, target planning, and fallout constraints that framed any general nuclear exchange in October 1962
documents.warQuestion: How did the U.S. plan to execute or limit nuclear strikes if a general war began?
documents.summary: A declassified SAC history of SIOP-63, including the move toward more flexible attack options, counterforce/no-cities concepts, strategic reserve forces, and unresolved command-and-control limits under nuclear-war conditions.
documents.repository: Mandatory Review release and appeal
documents.citation: Headquarters, Strategic Air Command, History and Research Division, History of the Joint Strategic Target Planning Staff: Preparation of SIOP-63, January 1964.
documents.sourceNote: Released through National Security Archive mandatory review appeals.

documents.title: Discussion at the 387th Meeting of the National Security Council
documents.evidenceRole: Shows the Net Evaluation Subcommittee method for estimating nuclear-war consequences
documents.warQuestion: What official machinery estimated deaths, destruction, and military effects in a general nuclear war?
documents.summary: Documents the NSC's use of net evaluations to estimate the effects of nuclear war on the United States, the Soviet Union, allies, civilian fatalities, economic resources, and military capabilities.
documents.repository: Dwight D. Eisenhower Library, Ann Whitman File, NSC Series, Box 10
documents.citation: Memorandum, Discussion at the 387th Meeting of the National Security Council, November 20, 1958.
documents.sourceNote: Posted as document 1 in the National Security Archive SIOP-62 release.

documents.title: Appraisal of Relative Merits of Alternative Retaliatory Efforts
documents.originator: JCS Chairman Nathan Twining / National Security Council
documents.evidenceRole: Shows target-system choices and the scale of destruction expected from nuclear retaliation
documents.warQuestion: What level of destruction did U.S. planners associate with prevailing in a nuclear exchange?
documents.summary: Reviews alternatives for retaliation against urban-industrial targets, military targets, and an optimum mix of both. The accompanying release context identifies the document as a key source for expected city destruction and mass casualties.
documents.repository: National Archives, RG 218, JCS Chairman Nathan Twining Papers, 381 Net Evaluation
documents.citation: Nathan Twining to Director, Joint Staff, Appraisal of Relative Merits of Alternative Retaliatory Efforts, February 19, 1960, enclosing memorandum to the President, February 12, 1960.
documents.sourceNote: Posted as document 4 in the National Security Archive SIOP-62 release.

documents.title: SAC Use of Computers in Targeting
documents.evidenceRole: Shows how the JSTPS constructed target lists and attack plans
documents.warQuestion: How would U.S. planners have matched nuclear weapons to Soviet-bloc targets?
documents.summary: Explains the practical targeting process behind SIOP-62, including desired ground zeroes, assumptions about high-yield weapons, and surface-burst planning that would have produced heavy fallout.
documents.repository: U.S. Navy Operational Archives, Arleigh Burke Papers, SIOP/NSTL Briefing Folder
documents.citation: Rear Adm. Paul Blackburn to Chief of Naval Operations, SAC Use of Computers in Targeting, October 26, 1960.
documents.sourceNote: Posted as document 13 in the National Security Archive SIOP-62 release.

documents.title: JCS Liaison Group Cable on SIOP Alert Force Planning
documents.originator: Gen. Berton E. Spivy, JCS Liaison Group
documents.evidenceRole: Shows alert-force size, target coverage, and execution assumptions
documents.warQuestion: What forces and target counts would a rapid U.S. nuclear strike have involved?
documents.summary: Reports on alert-force planning, delivery vehicles, weapons, targets, damage expectancy, and execution timing. It is one of the clearest declassified windows into how many weapons could be launched early in the plan.
documents.repository: U.S. Navy Operational Archives, Arleigh Burke Papers, SIOP/NSTL Briefing Folder
documents.citation: Gen. Berton E. Spivy, JCS Liaison Group, Offutt AFB, cable to JCS, October 29, 1960.
documents.sourceNote: Posted as document 14 in the National Security Archive SIOP-62 release.

documents.title: Review of the NSTL/SIOP-62 and Related Policy Guidance
documents.evidenceRole: Records senior objections that SIOP damage and population casualties were excessive
documents.warQuestion: Did U.S. officials understand that the war plan could produce destruction beyond military requirements?
documents.summary: Includes service-level critiques of SIOP-62 damage criteria, casualty levels, radiation assumptions, and the need to understand worldwide contamination effects.
documents.repository: National Archives, RG 218, Records of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, Decimal Files
documents.citation: Note by the Secretaries to the Joint Chiefs of Staff, Review of the NSTL/SIOP-62 and Related Policy Guidance, JCS 2056/197, December 30, 1960.
documents.sourceNote: Posted as document 19 in the National Security Archive SIOP-62 release.

documents.title: Strategic Target Planning
documents.evidenceRole: Captures White House science-adviser concerns about excessive force requirements
documents.warQuestion: What internal critiques existed before Kennedy inherited the SIOP?
documents.summary: Records George Kistiakowsky's review of SIOP-62 and the problems created by high assurance criteria, repeated weapons on the same targets, and limited presidential flexibility.
documents.repository: National Archives, RG 218, Records of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, Decimal Files
documents.citation: Note by the Secretaries to the Joint Chiefs of Staff on Strategic Target Planning, JCS 2056/208, January 27, 1961.
documents.sourceNote: Posted as document 23 in the National Security Archive SIOP-62 release.

documents.title: Secretary McNamara's Visit to the JSTPS
documents.evidenceRole: Shows McNamara's early confrontation with nuclear targeting and urban destruction
documents.warQuestion: What did the Defense Department know about how much force SIOP strikes would apply to cities and targets?
documents.summary: Documents McNamara's February 1961 visit to Offutt Air Force Base and questions about weapons, target coverage, urban-industrial targets, fallout, and damage levels.
documents.repository: FOIA release to National Security Archive
documents.citation: Memorandum for the Record, Secretary McNamara's Visit to the JSTPS, February 6, 1961.
documents.sourceNote: Posted as document 24B in the National Security Archive SIOP-62 release.

documents.title: Review of the NSTL/SIOP-62 and Related Policy Guidance
documents.evidenceRole: Shows the all-or-nothing character and China problem in early SIOP planning
documents.warQuestion: Could the United States easily withhold attacks on countries not directly involved in the crisis?
documents.summary: Includes high-level debate over whether the plan could avoid striking China or other targets if they were not involved, a core issue for any Cuba-triggered general war.
documents.repository: National Archives, RG 218, Records of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, Decimal Files
documents.citation: Note by the Secretaries to the Joint Chiefs of Staff, Review of the NSTL/SIOP-62 and Related Policy Guidance, JCS 2056/220, February 11, 1961.
documents.sourceNote: Posted as document 25 in the National Security Archive SIOP-62 release.

documents.title: JCLSG Offutt AFB Cable to JCS on SIOP-62 Updates
documents.evidenceRole: Gives aggregate weapons and desired ground zero counts for SIOP-62
documents.warQuestion: What order of magnitude of weapons and target points shaped the inherited plan?
documents.summary: Discloses aggregate SIOP-62 alert-force and committed-force weapons and designated ground zeroes, showing the scale of the plan Kennedy's administration sought to revise.
documents.repository: U.S. Navy Operational Archives, Arleigh Burke Papers
documents.citation: JCLSG, Offutt AFB cable 292318Z to JCS, April 28, 1961.
documents.sourceNote: Posted as document 27 in the National Security Archive SIOP-62 release.

documents.title: Transcript of a Meeting at the White House
documents.evidenceRole: First-day presidential discussion of air strike, invasion, warning, and Soviet response
documents.warQuestion: What choices did Kennedy's advisers first imagine once the missiles were confirmed?

documents.citation: Transcript of a Meeting at the White House, October 16, 1962, FRUS, 1961-1963, vol. XI, doc. 18.
documents.sourceNote: Source note in FRUS cites Kennedy Library presidential recordings, audiotape transcript.

documents.title: Off the Record Meeting on Cuba
documents.evidenceRole: Shows deeper first-day discussion of escalation, Berlin, and the costs of military action
documents.warQuestion: How did officials connect an attack on Cuba to a possible Berlin or global crisis?
documents.summary: A long off-the-record White House tape transcript in which Kennedy and advisers weighed whether a surprise attack or invasion would trigger Soviet counteraction and broader war.
documents.repository: Kennedy Library, President's Office Files, Presidential Recordings, Transcripts
documents.citation: Off the Record Meeting on Cuba, October 16, 1962, FRUS, 1961-1963, vol. XI, doc. 21.
documents.sourceNote: Source note in FRUS cites Kennedy Library presidential recordings, audiotapes 28.2 and 28A.1.

documents.title: Memorandum of Meeting

documents.warQuestion: What did the intelligence and national security principals think the military choices were?

documents.repository: CIA DCI/McCone Files
documents.citation: Memorandum of Meeting, October 17, 1962, FRUS, 1961-1963, vol. XI, doc. 22.
documents.sourceNote: Source note in FRUS cites CIA DCI/McCone Files, Job 80-B01285A.

documents.title: Letter From Adlai Stevenson to President Kennedy
documents.evidenceRole: Provides a primary alternative to immediate force based on escalation risk
documents.warQuestion: What arguments inside the administration stressed negotiation to avoid a war path?
documents.summary: Stevenson's warning against immediate air strikes and his proposed diplomatic alternatives help define the fork between coercive diplomacy and direct military action.

documents.citation: Adlai Stevenson to President Kennedy, October 17, 1962, FRUS, 1961-1963, vol. XI, doc. 25.
documents.sourceNote: Source note in FRUS cites Kennedy Library National Security Files, Countries Series, Cuba.

documents.title: Record of Meeting
documents.evidenceRole: Shows State/Defense/CIA discussion of blockade, air strike, invasion, and likely consequences
documents.warQuestion: How did the principals compare the likely consequences of the main U.S. options?
documents.summary: A high-value record of policy principals discussing the costs and uncertainties of quarantine, air attack, and invasion before Kennedy selected the public quarantine path.
documents.repository: Department of State, S/S Files, Lot 65 D 438
documents.citation: Record of Meeting, October 19, 1962, FRUS, 1961-1963, vol. XI, doc. 31.
documents.sourceNote: Source note in FRUS cites Department of State S/S Files, Cuba Week Drafts.

documents.title: SNIE 11-18-62: Soviet Reactions to Certain U.S. Courses of Action on Cuba
documents.evidenceRole: Core estimate of whether U.S. military action would escalate to general war
documents.warQuestion: How did U.S. intelligence estimate Soviet retaliation if the United States attacked Cuba?
documents.summary: The key intelligence estimate on likely Soviet reaction to warning, blockade, air attack, or invasion. It explicitly considered whether military action could produce a chain of action and reaction leading to general war.
documents.repository: Department of State, S/S Files, Lot 65 D 438, CIA-Cuba
documents.citation: Special National Intelligence Estimate 11-18-62, Soviet Reactions to Certain U.S. Courses of Action on Cuba, October 19, 1962, FRUS, 1961-1963, vol. XI, doc. 32.

documents.title: Minutes of the 505th Meeting of the National Security Council
documents.evidenceRole: Shows the President's formal comparison of quarantine and military attack

documents.title: Notes on Meeting With President Kennedy

documents.summary: McNamara's notes record the planned sortie structure, the uncertain ability to destroy all missiles, the estimate that some missiles were operational, and the judgment that air strikes would lead inevitably to invasion.
documents.repository: Washington National Records Center, RG 330, OASD(C) A Files

documents.sourceNote: Source note in FRUS cites WNRC RG 330 OASD(C) files; also reproduced in CIA Documents on the Cuban Missile Crisis.

documents.repository: Kennedy Library, National Security Files, Meetings and Memoranda Series, NSC Meetings

documents.citation: Memorandum from the Acting Chairman of the Board of National Estimates to DCI McCone, October 23, 1962, FRUS, 1961-1963, vol. XI, doc. 54.
